title: The effects of cooling via compressed air on geometrical, mechanical and microstructural properties of 600 MPa high strength steel walls manufactured by CMT WAAM
abstract: Abstract In this study, the effects of compressed air cooling (CAC) and free cooling (FC) applied between the layers of the walls fabricated by cold metal transfer wire arc additive manufacturing (CMT-WAAM) process on the microstructural changes and the effects of these changes on the mechanical properties using high strength (minimum 600 MPa) steel wire were investigated. Neither shielding gas nor special tooling was utilized. Compressed air gun in the workshop was used to supply compressed air. The wall obtained with FC was wider (21%) and higher (7%), while the average sidewall roughness (waviness) values were 128% higher than the CACed wall. The results showed that the cooling rate had a decisive influence on the microstructure; CAC promoted the formation of lower bainite and martensite/austenite (M/A) phases, leading to a significant increase in strength values. On the other hand, FC led to the formation of upper bainite and increased inclusion density, which partially negatively affected the mechanical strength. CAC resulted in a 124% and 47% increase in average yield and tensile strength, respectively. The CACed WAAM walls showed higher hardness values in all regions compared to the FCed ones, especially in the upper wall region, where the hardness was measured to be 288 ± 14 HV 0.2  compared to 171 ± 7 HV 0.2  for the FCed wall. Notch impact tests at − 20 °C and − 50 °C revealed a 17.5% and 10.8% reduction in toughness of the CACed walls compared to the FCed walls, respectively, but the ductile fracture behavior was maintained in both cases.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Large metallic parts with medium complexity can be manufactured quickly thanks to directed energy deposition (DED) techniques, which use concentrated heat energy to melt the feedstock material [ 1 ]. Wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) is included in DED additive manufacturing (AM) category, such as wire laser additive manufacturing (WLAM) [ 2 ], laser arc hybrid additive manufacturing (LAHAM) [ 3 ], plasma wire arc additive manufacturing (PWAAM) [ 4 ] etc. and in this method, the wire electrode is generally melted with arc energy, layers are deposited and near-net-shape part is obtained [ 5 ]. Even without any additional processing, selective laser melting (SLM) and selective laser sintering (SLS), AM methods can fabricate more detailed parts with higher surface quality and dimensional accuracy than those obtained with WAAM [ 6 ]. One of the reasons for this difference is high heat input in the WAAM method compared with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processes. This heat input can create undesirable melt pools in some places, which can disrupt the layer structure and surface quality [ 7 ]. One of the biggest disadvantages of SLS and SLM methods is that the amount of metal deposition (~ 0.1–0.6 kg.h −1 ) is very limited and the printing time is long. In contrast, with WAAM, it is possible to deposit large quantities of metal (~ 3–8 kg.h −1 ) much more cheaply and easily [ 8 ]. Many engineering materials (titanium, nickel, aluminum and steel and alloys of these metals, etc.) are suitable to be printed (built) with WAAM and this reduces the manufacturing time by 40–60% and additional processing time by 15–20%. This process is also suitable for the manufacturing of larger parts in high numbers because it has a higher manufacturing speed, since the part sizes in SLS and SLM methods are very limited due to the need to print the parts in a closed chamber and a protective gas atmosphere [ 9 ].

In addition to having significant mechanical qualities, ultra-high-strength steels (UHSS), which have yield strengths more than 690 N∙mm −2 , have been in high demand to meet energy efficiency and lightweight structure requirements. UHSS have been used by the transportation, pipeline, offshore, and shipbuilding industries and by vehicles such as trucks and cranes [ 10 ,  11 ]. Conventionally, UHSS could be optimized for strength, toughness, and ductility by fine-tuning their chemical composition and managing thermomechanical processes. UHSS are obtained via thermomechanical (TM) rolling with rapid cooling and quenching and tempering (Q + T) [ 12 ].

WAAM of high strength low alloy (HSLA), advanced high strength steels (AHSS) and UHSS have been studied by some researchers. Fang et al. [ 13 ] focused on fabrication of 800 MPa HSLA steel via WAAM and they investigated room and elevated temperature (600 °C) tensile properties and corresponding microstructures. In another study by Dirisu et al., fracture toughness and failure modes of HSLA steel structures deposited by WAAM using oscillating and stringer passes and three different HSLA steel wires (ER70S-6, ER90S-B3, ER120S-G) were analyzed [ 14 ]. Using ER70S feedstock wire, Nemani et al. [ 15 ] investigated the viability of fabricating a typically rolled low-carbon low-alloy shipbuilding steel plate using WAAM method. Both conventionally rolled and WAAM samples were subjected to various heat treatment cycles after the fabrication process, such as air-cooling and water-quenching from the intercritical austenitizing temperature of 800 °C. The WAAMed ship plate's microstructure was found to be homogenized by air-cooling heat treatment, which resulted in a minor reduction in hardness and tensile strength. Meanwhile, the water-quenching cycle yielded acicular ferrite and intergranular pearlite, which enhanced the part's mechanical qualities. Babu et al. [ 16 ] tried to control mechanical properties of S690 grade high strength steel locally and they employed high heat input and low heat input regions (layers) in turn and obtained functional grading. Researchers [ 17 ] utilized ER70S-6 wire to build walls with WAAM and applied interlayer delays (i.e., 40 s, 80 s and 120 s). They examined bead geometry and hardness in deposited walls with different interlayer pauses. Meng et al. [ 18 ] investigated geometrical characteristics, mechanical properties and microstructure of the WAAM walls deposited inside a salt bath furnace set at 200 °C using welding wire with minimum 890 MPa yield strength. WAAM has the potential to be an alternative manufacturing technique to conventional ones if parameters are properly controlled. During WAAM, in-situ strengthening of a deposited wall using ER110S-G high strength low alloy steel wire via addition of SiC particles was researched by Rodrigues et al. [ 19 ]. They noted increase in mechanical strength due to refined grains and fine dispersion of cementite as a result of SiC dissociation.

The main objectives of cooling in welding are to prevent an uneven melt pool, which is also a disadvantage of WAAM, and to improve the final mechanical properties. By increasing the cooling rate, the solidification rate will increase and in parallel, heat build-up will decrease, which is expected to reduce issues such as seam sagging and distortion. When the studies on cooling are examined, it is seen that most studies are on cooling with a shielding gas (Ar, CO 2 , etc.), which is also common in conventional welding methods. Studies involving cooling and the use of pressurized gas during interlayer waiting are very rare. Badoniya et al. [ 20 ] researched the effect of interlayer waiting time (i.e., 1 to 4 min) on microstructure and mechanical performance of WAAM fabricated 316 L stainless steel. Tonelli et al. [ 21 ] investigated interlayer active air cooling in order to mitigate waiting times between deposition of each layer in manufacturing of 304L austenitic stainless steel and its effect on mechanical properties and microstructure. Reindl et al. [ 22 ] examined the effects of preheating via heating plate and cobot guided inductor and active (i.e. water) cooling in WAAM of steel and aluminum on the hardness, microstructure, and dimensional accuracy. Da Silva et al. studied near-immersion active cooling (NIAC) in WAAM of ER5356 aluminum alloy and looked into concept validation and the effects of layer edge to water distance and polarity (electrode positive to electrode negative ratio) on porosity level and geometric features of the walls [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. Soliman et al. [ 26 ] compared natural cooling and interlayer nitrogen cooling in WAAM of 5356 Al–Mg alloy and their effects on microstructure and mechanical properties of the walls fabricated. In another study on WAAM of Al–Mg alloy, researchers focused on the effectiveness of fast cooling via vortex tube and water cooling base and compared it with natural cooling. Dash et al. [ 27 ] researched manufacturing of cylindrical shaped steel parts using ER70S-6 wire with and without active cooling (heat exchanger fixed on the CNC table) in hybrid WAAM. They concluded that active cooling reduced volumetric/surface defects by a quite significant amount of 99%. Microstructure of the parts was homogeneous and consisted of polygonal ferrite grains and pearlites. Researchers also noted an increase in hardness with active cooling. Heat accumulation from layer-by-layer depositions raises the temperature of the layer that was previously deposited during WAAM. Process instabilities occur from this, which alter material properties and yield deviations from the required dimension.

CMT process is known to be very low heat input welding method compared with conventional GMAW with the help of highly controlled wire feed and arc. Overflow of the layers due to high heat input, not only degrades mechanical properties but also geometric accuracy of the parts, which yield longer machining times and increase in cost. In this study, the effect of interlayer CAC on mechanical and microstructural properties of a wall obtained by CMT WAAM using 600 MPa yield strength steel wire was researched and compared with a wall fabricated by waiting in the air (FC) for 30 s between layers deposited. Main motivation was to investigate the applicability of interlayer CAC rather than a costly shielding gas in order to increase cooling rate after deposition and solidification of the layers in WAAM of HSLA steel with 600 MPa yield strength and fill the gap in the literature in this respect.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs:
Two walls with a length of 350 mm and a design height of 110 mm were obtained with 3 passes overlapped side by side (approx. width 10 ~ 11 mm). There was 30 s waiting time after deposition of each layer for the first wall (FC) and the second wall was cooled for 30 s with compressed air after deposition of each layer. Layer height was 1.4 mm and total number of layers deposited was 80. Substrate was a low carbon steel. The GMAW wire used (Table  1 ) is classified as G  69 A 2 U M N3M2 according to EN ISO 16834-B:2007, ER100S-G according to AWS A5.28–05 and has a diameter of 1.2 mm. Ar + 18%CO 2  (EN ISO 14175-M21) mixture gas was used as shielding gas; gas flow rate was 15 l.min −1 . The wire stick-out was set to 18 mm. The arc welding robot was a Fanuc Arc Mate 100iD and the welding machine was a Fronius TPS 600i (Fig.  1 a) and the layers were deposited in CMT mode and in PA position (torch angle 88° in push position) and at a welding speed of 400 mm.min −1 . The welding current intensity was 93 A, arc voltage 10.9 V and wire feed speed 2.1 m.min −1  and raster build strategy was implemented [ 28 ]. Detailed parameters are given in Table  2 . WAAM walls deposited are presented in Fig.  1 b–c.

All testing equipment was accredited. Tests were realized in a temperature-controlled room (24.6 °C room temperature, 53.6% relative humidity recorded by accredited Testo 622 thermohygrometer). All of the tensile and Charpy impact test and macro–micro-hardness characterization specimen were extracted from middle section of the deposited walls, where the process was much stabilized. Specimen extraction areas and actual WAAM walls deposited are presented in Fig.  2 . Small tensile test specimens [two horizontal and two vertical per region (i.e., upper, middle and lower) and a total of 12 per wall], whose dimensions (30 × 8 × 2 mm 3 ) were designed in accordance with ASTM STP 1329 [ 29 ], were prepared via machining according to ISO 6892–1 [ 30 ] standard. Room temperature tests were carried out in accordance with ISO 4136 [ 31 ] utilizing TIME WDW-10 M tensile test machine. In upper, middle and lower regions of the walls, four Charpy V-notch impact test specimens (with dimensions 55 × 10 × 2.5 mm 3 ) per region (i.e., upper, middle and lower) were extracted from the walls according to EN ISO 9016 [ 32 ] and V-notches were machined through-height of the walls. Zwick Roell RKP300 Charpy tester with a capacity of 300 J was utilized to perform impact tests at − 20 °C and − 50 °C temperatures according to ISO 148–1 [ 33 ]. Sub-zero temperatures were achieved using 99.5% pure grade acetone and dry ice and using accredited CHY RTD 505 digital thermometer for temperature measurements. Vickers microhardness test specimens were extracted along the height of the walls and hardness tests were performed using the Vickers hardness tester with a 200gf load (HV 0.2 ) in accordance with EN 6507–1 [ 34 ] and EN 9015–2 [ 35 ] from upper region to lower region of the specimens. Hardness maps of each region (i.e., upper, middle, lower) were plotted using hardness data obtained from 50 measurements (5 × 10 measurements in a grid corresponding to a 2.5 mm × 5 mm area) in MATLAB 2023b. Microstructure specimens were also extracted from middle section of the walls and they were ground using SiC papers, polished using 3 μm and 1 μm diamond compounds and etched with Nital (3% vol.) solutions. Zeiss Axio Scope.A1 optical microscope (OM) was utilized to obtain microstructure images and fracture surfaces of tensile test and notch impact specimens and also microstructure specimens were analyzed using field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) (FEI Quanta FEG 450). Zeiss SmartZoom 5 automated digital microscope was used for profile measurements (waviness) of side walls and three measurements were realized (2 measurements on left side wall and 1 measurement on right side wall). Specimens and test equipment utilized in the tests and characterization are presented in Fig.  3 . sections.heading: Macro geometry
paragraphs: Macro images of CACed and FCed WAAM walls are given in Fig.  4 . FCed wall is much rougher and not as straight as the one obtained with compressed air cooling. FCed wall also has porosity near the substrate. Wall widths, heights and effective areas for CACed and FCed walls are 9.7 mm and 11.8 mm; 98.8 mm and 106.1 mm; and 958.36 mm 2  and 1251.98 mm 2 , respectively. It depicts that FCed wall has more width (21%), height (7%) and effective area (30%) compared with CACed wall. It is apparent that FCed wall needs more machining to reach final shape and effective wall area, whereas CACed wall is near net shape. Fig. 4 Wall heights, widths and effective areas of CACed (left) and FCed (right) WAAM walls

sections.heading: Side wall surface waviness evaluation
paragraphs: As seen in Fig.  2  and Fig.  4 , there is a significant difference easily observable in side wall waviness between the CACed and FCed WAAM walls. Figure  5  and Fig.  6  present three surface profile measurements in FCed and CACed WAAM walls using digital microscope, respectively. Peaks in FCed wall are much higher and valleys are much deeper compared with CACed wall. Figure  7  shows side wall surface waviness (SW) values of WAAM walls obtained with CAC and FC. Fig. 5 Surface profile (surface waviness) measurements of FCed WAAM wall Fig. 6 Surface profile (surface waviness) measurements of CACed WAAM wall Fig. 7 Side wall surface waviness values of CAC and FC WAAM walls

Figure  8  visualizes and summarizes surface waviness results obtained by different researchers, who employed low and high heat input or utilization of different processes. Fig. 8 Comparison of surface waviness values with other researchers [ 18 ,  37 ,  38 ,  39 – 40 ]

In study of Meng et al. [ 18 ], surface waviness values of WAAM walls obtained using ER120S-G wire, were 1350 µm with air cooling and 1750 µm with isothermal salt bath treatment, which depicted 23% reduction. Rodideal et al. [ 37 ] applied two different heat inputs (i.e., low and high) in depositing WAAM walls using welding wire with minimum 890 MPa yield strength. Researchers obtained 597 ± 88 µm and 660 ± 143 µm with low and high heat inputs, respectively. Again, low heat input yielded 9.5% in reduction of surface waviness. In a study by Fonseca et al. (2024) [ 38 ], WAAM walls were obtained with conventional and hot forged variants using 710 MPa yield strength steel. They obtained average surface waviness values of 600 µm for conventional and 1210 µm for hot forged WAAM processes. Hot forging resulted in doubling the surface waviness. Dahat et al. [ 39 ] employed CMT and utilized metal cored wire with 690 MPa minimum yield strength in order to build WAAM walls and compressed air by a vortex tube was applied to cool down each layers after deposition. Researchers applied three different heat inputs (i.e., low, medium and high) and they acquired 510 µm (lowest) and 640 µm (highest) SW values with medium and low heat inputs, respectively. Lowering heat input yielded 20% reduction in SW. In another study, Fonseca et al. (2022) [ 40 ] maintained equal low heat input (221 J.mm −1 ) in depositing WAAM walls using ER110S-G wire with conventional and hot forging processes and they acquired SW values of 997 µm and 1210 µm with conventional and hot forged WAAM processes, respectively. Hot forging resulted in 21% increase in SW.

As seen in Fig.  7 , CAC led to 178 µm average SW, whereas, FC caused average SW of 406 µm. These measurements indicate a noteworthy 56% reduction in SW. CAC yielded a wall, where surface waviness as low as 95 µm was achieved in an individual measurement.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: OM and SEM images of the walls obtained using CAC are shown in Fig.  9  and Fig.  10 . As the weld metal microstructure transforms from austenite to ferrite and carbides with different morphologies, high cooling rates lead to the formation of martensite or lower bainite (B L ), while slower cooling rates promote the formation of upper bainite (B U ) [ 41 ]. The mechanical properties of the upper bainite are lower than the lower bainite [ 42 ]. Due to the low heat input provided by the CMT process, a higher cooling rate compared to conventional arc welding, supported by a simultaneous cooling process, favored the formation of lower bainite (Fig.  9 ). When cooled rapidly to temperatures close to room temperature, any remaining austenite can be fully or partially transformed into martensite. This mixture of martensite-austenite phases is called the M/A constituent [ 43 ]. The M/A constituent, which exists as a continuous and interconnected structure, is detrimental to toughness [ 44 ]. In the reheated regions, M/A formations (dark areas) within the bainitic matrix structure are noticeable. While a more uniform and denser M/A distribution was observed in the upper region of the CACed wall, a more columnar and sparse formation was exhibited in the lower region (Fig.  10 ). Fig. 9 Upper region microstructure of the CACed wall. OM and SEM images of the weld metal (a-b-c), and the reheated zone (d-e–f) Fig. 10 Lower region microstructure of the CACed wall. OM and SEM images of the weld metal (a-b-c), and the reheated zone (d-e–f)

Figures  11  and  12  show OM and SEM images of the wall obtained under FC conditions (30 s waiting between layer depositions). The presence of more intense inclusion formation in both the upper and lower regions compared to the CACed wall microstructures is noteworthy. Increased cooling time allowed the precipitation of inclusions. The formation of the upper bainite was ensured by the absence of CAC, which reduced the retention time in the bainitization temperature range. The upper bainite forms at higher temperatures, which allows the excess carbon to partition before precipitation in the ferrite [ 45 ]. It is inevitable that in the case of weld metal that remains in the bainitization temperature range for a long time due to FC, the upper bainite, which leads to lower strength than the lower bainite, will have a partially negative effect on the mechanical properties. sections.heading: Notch impact test
paragraphs: The notch impact test results of specimens extracted from CACed and FCed WAAM walls tested at − 20 °C and − 50 °C are given in Fig.  13 . According to the results obtained, the test temperature does not have a significant effect on toughness properties. In the upper, middle and lower regions, where the specimens were taken, the changes are not very sharp when the standard deviations are taken into account. Compared to the FCed wall, the notch impact results of the CACed wall, in which the lower bainite + M/A constituent is dominant, exhibited an average decrease of 17.5% and 10.8% for the temperatures − 20 °C and − 50 °C, respectively. Considering the effect of the lower bainite and M/A constituent, especially on toughness, this is expected and quite low. It is inferred quite high toughness values will be obtained at larger wall thicknesses, considering that the results of the specimens prepared in 55*10*2.5 mm 3  size due to the wall thickness of the WAAM wall. Figure  14  and Fig.  15  present SEM images of the fracture surfaces of the specimens. The walls with bainitic microstructure tested at − 20 °C and − 50 °C exhibited a ductile network fracture that met the minimum toughness requirements in all cases. All specimens have a pronounced lateral expansion. Images taken at the beginning, middle and end of fracture show no evidence of any semi-ductile or brittle structure. Fig. 13 Impact test results of specimens extracted from CAC and FC WAAM walls tested at − 20 °C and − 50 °C Fig. 14 Fracture surface images of V-notch impact test specimens (upper region) tested at − 20 °C (top: CAC; bottom: FC) ((a) Fracture initiation region, (b) Unstable fracture region, (c) Final fracture region) Fig. 15 Fracture surface images of V-notch impact test specimens (upper region) tested at − 50 °C (top: CAC; bottom: FC) (( a ) Fracture initiation region, ( b ) Unstable fracture region, ( c ) Final fracture region)

sections.heading: Tensile test
paragraphs:
Tensile strength, yield strength and % elongation results obtained by tensile tests are given in Table  3 . In addition, the graphs of the data obtained from the upper and lower regions are shown in Fig.  16 . The effect of CAC is clearly seen both in Table  3  and Fig.  16 . The lower bainite and M/A constituent obtained as a result of CAC, which develops at lower austenite transformation temperatures and generally faster cooling rates compared to the upper bainite, led to a significant increase in strength. The average tensile, yield strength and elongation values of the wall obtained by CAC were 791.8 ± 15.08 MPa, 622.6 ± 33.05 MPa and 26.63 ± 2.63%, respectively, while the values for FCed walls were 537.1 ± 12.35 MPa, 277.6 ± 8.15 MPa and 34.5 ± 2.57%, respectively.

Based on average values, the yield strength of the wall obtained under FC conditions decreased by 55.4% and tensile strength by 32.2%, while elongation values increased by 29.5%. Since the tensile tests were performed with horizontal and vertical axes, the CAC horizontal specimens showed a 1.1% decrease in tensile strength (compared to vertical specimens), a 5.8% decrease in yield strength and a 4% increase in elongation. Considering the horizontal specimens compared to the vertical specimens, the yield and tensile values showed an insignificant change (~ 1%) under FC conditions, while the elongation values increased by 5%. The fact that the grains in the bainitic structure are not formed in long needle or lath structures limited the direction-dependent mechanical property changes.

The fracture surfaces of the horizontal and vertical tensile test specimens taken from the upper region of the walls after the tests under CAC and FC conditions are given in Fig.  17 . After fracture, the cross-sectional areas of the specimens under CAC conditions, which have higher mechanical properties, have a larger area than the specimen under FC conditions. Cross-sectional reductions were calculated using an imaging software. In horizontal specimens, the cross-sectional reduction of CACH 1–1 was 38%, while the cross-sectional reduction of FCH 4–1 was 49%. In vertical specimens, the cross-sectional reduction of CACV 1–1 was 34%, while the cross-sectional reduction of FCV 4–1 was 58%. Since the specimen orientation did not have a significant effect on the strength, similar cross-sectional reduction results were obtained under the same cooling conditions. The fracture surfaces consist of a network structure formed as a result of the rupture of fine grains. Due to the similar elongation values and similar microstructure (only different types of bainite), no significant differences were detected in fracture surfaces. sections.heading: Vickers hardness
paragraphs: Vickers hardness maps of upper, middle and lower regions of CACed and FCed WAAM walls are presented in Fig.  18  and Fig.  19 , respectively. CACed wall is significantly harder than FCed wall in all regions. In CACed wall, upper region is the hardest zone (288 ± 14 HV 0.2 ) followed by middle region (285 ± 10) and then lower region (273 ± 11 HV 0.2 ). In FCed wall, upper region is softest zone (171 ± 7 HV 0.2 ) and it is followed by middle region (186 ± 8 HV 0.2 ) and lower region (191 ± 8 HV 0.2 ). In FCed wall, substrate sinks the heat easily at the beginning of the deposition of the first layers, which leads to higher cooling rate but then substrate is saturated with heat and cannot absorb more, which leads to lower cooling rate. As the heat builds up in the wall, cooling rates for middle and upper regions become slower, which yield softening and low hardness values. On the other hand, CAC helped the wall dissipate heat effectively and there was no significant tempering effect of the previous layer, as in FC, which yielded higher hardness values. Under CAC conditions (e.g., the CMT effect with CAC and low heat input), finer lower bainite and transformation products such as M/A have formed. These phases increase hardness due to higher dislocation density. Additionally, the presence of M/A components has created locally high-hardness regions. Under FC conditions, however, the formation of upper bainite is dominant due to slower cooling. Since upper bainite has a coarser structure and elongated cementite layers, it exhibits lower hardness values compared to lower bainite. Fig. 18 Vickers hardness maps of upper, middle and lower regions of CACed WAAM wall Fig. 19 Vickers hardness maps of upper, middle and lower regions of FCed WAAM wall

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: WAAM walls were fabricated by GMAW method and in CMT mode, with three overlapping passes and 80 layers. In the first wall, FC was applied between the layers, while in the second wall, CAC was applied for 30 s after deposition of each layer. The data obtained at the end of the tests and characterizations are summarized as follows. CAC reduced the SW by 56% to an average value of 178 µm, reaching as low as 95 µm in some places. Microstructure images of the CACed walls indicate that high cooling rate due to CAC promoted the formation of lower bainite (B L ) and in some areas martensite/austenite (M/A) constituents. FC led to the formation of upper bainite (B U ) with lower strength because of lower cooling rate. CAC resulted in a finer microstructure, while slow cooling yielded a coarser structure accompanied by inclusion formation. In terms of toughness values, the wall CACed and dominated by the B L  + M/A constituent showed a 17.5% and 10.8% decrease in toughness for temperatures of − 20 °C and − 50 °C, respectively, compared to the FCed wall. CAC increased the tensile and yield strengths of the microstructure containing B L  and M/A by 47% and 124%, respectively, while the elongation decreased by about 23% compared to FC. In every region, CACed walls are substantially harder than FCed ones (i.e., 68% for upper region, 53% for middle region, 43% for lower region). Specimen orientation (i.e., vertical or horizontal) has no significant effect on strength in FCed walls. CACed specimens in vertical orientation presented a minor increase (up to 6%) in average strength and elongation (1.5%). No significant difference was observed in fracture surfaces due to similar microstructure and elongation values. Ductile network structure dominates the overall morphology. In WAAM of HSLA steel, it is advised to utilize CAC in order to improve mechanical properties and decrease surface waviness and cost via reduction in machining and shielding gas needs.
